newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak FinMin plans larger 1997 budget deficit.
newsitem.headline: Slovak FinMin plans larger 1997 budget deficit.

text.p: The Slovak finance ministry on Tuesday presented revised plans for the draft 1997 state budget, increasing its planned overall deficit to 30 billion Slovak crowns ($959.7 million) from an originally forecast 25 billion crowns.

Budget revenues would total some 170 billion crowns, down from the previously announced 175 billion crowns, about 15.9 billion crowns more than in 1996, according to the ministry proposal presented to the government and obtained by Reuters.
Plans for budget expenditure remained unchanged at 200 billion crowns, some 10 billion crowns more than in 1996. The 1996 state budget deficit is planned to total 27 billion crowns.

In the first seven months of 1996, the budget deficit totalled 6.08 billion crowns, but government officials have said revenues might get tighter later in the year due to lower than expected tax income.

Slovakia has been showing some of the best basic economic indicators in post-communist Europe. Inflation was at 5.6 percent year-on-year in August, compared with 9.8 percent in the same month last year. GDP grew 7.4 percent in calendar 1995 and 7.1 percent in the January-June period of this year.
The 1997 budget proposal is based on the assumption that gross domestic product (GDP) will grow at least five percent in 1997 and inflation will be kept under six percent.
According to this forecast, the country's GDP is expected to total 650 billion crowns in 1997. The overall deficit should then represent 4.6 percent of the GDP.
But according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) standards the 1997 fiscal deficit should total only some 8.6 billion crowns, which is 1.32 percent of the forecast GDP.
In 1996 the fiscal deficit calculated according to IMF standards is planned to total some 14.4 billion crowns, or 2.5 percent of the GDP.
According to preliminary plans, expenditures for debt servicing should total around 35.3 billion crowns, 3.4 billion crowns more than the planned sum for 1996.
The finance ministry has proposed a strategy under which the country's debt should be assessed as a proportion of GDP.
"This means that even if the total debt increases, the upward trend should be slower than GDP growth," the ministry report said.
The ministry document said the government should discuss the complete draft on the 1997 state budget on November 12, and should presented it to parliament by November 15.
